Build the row-per-interval table a failure-rate model is fitted to

Source: R/discrete-time-hazard-brms.R
build_hazard_data.Rd

Reshapes one row per individual, together with a temperature trajectory, into one row per individual and at-risk interval. An interval-censored failure gives the failure its whole censoring interval; a known-time one truncates the final at-risk interval at the recorded time. The cumulative hazard is integrated numerically over the at-risk intervals, with the failure-check times serving as the integration nodes. For a known-time failure, the fit integrates on the checks (its final interval ending exactly at the failure time) and no finer sub-grid is required but can be provided.

Usage

build_hazard_data(
  ind,
  path,
  observation = c("interval", "continuous", "mixed"),
  covariates = character(0),
  Tr = NULL,
  tau_ref = NULL,
  checks = NULL,
  grid_dt = NULL,
  grid_dT = 0.1,
  costressors = list()
)

Arguments

ind

A data frame with one row per individual. Required: id, path_id (key into path), event (1 = failed, 0 = right-censored), plus the covariate columns referenced in the model. Timing depends on how the failure was observed: interval-censored individuals have t_upper (the check at which failure was found, or a survivor's last observed check); known-time ones have t_event (the known time of failure or censoring). For observation = "mixed" the data also needs an obs_type column per individual ("interval" or "continuous"), and each type supplies its own timing column. Every individual is taken to be at risk from time 0 of its path: the table has no entry time, so an individual that joins an exposure after it began cannot be represented.

path

A data frame giving the temperature trajectory for each path. Required columns: path_id, time, temp. The function interpolates these points linearly in time, so a minimal two-point path (start and end) encodes a linear ramp, and each path has one reading at each time: a sudden change is written as two readings a moment apart (e.g., at 10 and 10.01). Interpolation uses the full series, so a temperature data logger whose records are finer than the checks still supplies the true temperature at each interval midpoint (never a check-to-check straight line); the checks control only the integration grid, not the temperature. Temperatures outside the recorded time range are held flat at the nearest endpoint rather than returned as NA, because the at-risk grid (the checks, the exact failure time, and the t = 0 start) need not sit strictly inside the logged times: a check or failure time can fall just past the last reading, or the first interval can begin before the first reading, and an NA temperature there would propagate into Ta and the linear predictor.

observation

How each failure time was observed. One of "interval" (every failure known only to fall within a censoring interval), "continuous" (every failure observed at a known time), or "mixed" (both kinds in one table, each individual's kind given by its obs_type column). This determines which response family the table is fitted with, and whether the exact flag is added; the response column is failed in every mode.

covariates

A character vector of column names in ind to carry through onto every row of the output table, so they are available in the model formula as fixed-effect predictors or as grouping factors for random effects. A trial identifier is the common case: include it here, then place a trial-level random intercept on a parameter in build_hazard_spec, e.g. dpar_formulas = list(loga = ~ 1 + (1 | trial)). The individual identifier id is always kept, so an individual-level grouping term needs no entry here.

Tr

The reference temperature, written to a constant Tr column so the functions can form Ta - Tr. It is a single model reference, not the per-trial starting temperature (see M_catalogue); the per-trial starts live in the temperature trajectories (path). For the forms that take a logarithm or fractional power of Ta - Tr (zeroexp, power, zeropower) it is the temperature at which the rate is zero (or, for power, falls to its baseline), so it must be given, at or below the coldest temperature in the data. Otherwise it defaults (NULL) to the median temperature at which failures were observed, which places loga where the data are and keeps it from being tied to the thermal sensitivity b; a reference far from the failures makes the two hard to tell apart. It must be set to a common value across datasets when comparing loga, whose meaning is anchored at Tr.

tau_ref

A single positive number, the reference time, in the time unit of the data, written to a constant tau_ref column. The scale of the weibull baseline is fixed at it (see h0_catalogue), and the default priors of the parameters that depend on the time unit are scaled by it (see build_hazard_prior). It defaults (NULL) to the median time at which failures were observed, which places loga where the data are, as the default Tr does. A reference time much longer than the times at which individuals fail makes loga an extrapolation in time that depends heavily on the shape of the baseline. Like Tr, set it to a common value across datasets when comparing loga under a weibull baseline, whose meaning is anchored at it.

checks

An optional data frame with path_id, time giving the failure-check schedule per path (i.e., the times at which each individual was inspected for failure). Defaults to the distinct path times (logger reading = check). Time 0, the start of the exposure, is added to every schedule when it is not listed. An interval-censored t_upper must be one of its path's checks: a time between two checks, or past the last one, is refused. As noted above, these times double as the integration nodes for the cumulative hazard, so their spacing sets the midpoint-rule resolution. For a known-time failure, a regular grid can be used instead (see grid_dt).

grid_dt

An optional numeric giving a fixed time step (in the units of path$time). If set, a known-time failure is followed on a regular grid of this step, from t = 0 to the failure time, instead of on checks. Defaults to NULL (the checks, or the readings of path). Either way the intervals are divided further where grid_dT requires it.

grid_dT

A single positive number, the largest change in temperature allowed within an interval at risk, in degrees. An interval over which temperature changes by more is divided into equal parts (see The time grid). Defaults to 0.1; Inf keeps the intervals as given.

costressors

An optional list of costressor objects declaring non-temperature stressors (dissolved oxygen and the like). Each adds a standardised column z_<name>, read from its own trajectory (interpolated to the interval midpoints) or, for a stressor held fixed within a trial, from a column of ind. Defaults to none.

Value

A long-format data frame, one row per individual and at-risk interval, holding the identifiers id and path_id; the model columns Ta, Tr, tau, log_tau, tau_ref, exposure, log_exposure; the carried covariates; one z_<name> column per co-stressor; the 0/1 response column failed; and, for mixed observation, the integer exact flag the family branches on.

The time grid

Within each interval at risk the hazard is taken as constant, at its value at the midpoint of the interval. That is accurate while temperature changes little within the interval, because the failure rate rises steeply with temperature. With a thermal sensitivity of b = 1.7 per degree, for example, the rate is exp(1.7 x 0.1) = 1.19 times higher at the end of an interval that spans 0.1 degrees than at its start, and exp(1.7 x 0.5) = 2.3 times higher across one that spans half a degree; the hazard accrued over the interval, taken at its midpoint, is then understated by about (b dT)^2 / 24, that is by 0.1% over a tenth of a degree and by 3% over half a degree, an error that grows with the square of the change in temperature. So any interval over which temperature changes by more than grid_dT is divided into equal parts, each with its own row; a part that still changes by more, where the path bends within the interval (a logged record, or a ramp held and then resumed), is divided again; and a message says how many rows resulted.

The error left by the default step grows with the square of b. In simulations of large ramping assays (eight assays of 3,000 individuals at three ramp rates, fitted by maximum likelihood), the default of 0.1 degrees raised b and the Weibull shape by about 0.1% at b = 1.7 and by about 1% at b = 4.7, and sCTmax by 0.007 degrees at b = 4.7; dCTmax was not affected. Those are small against the uncertainty of an assay of a hundred or so individuals. Where the fitted b is above about 3, a step of 0.05 makes them about four times smaller, at the cost of twice the rows and about twice the time to fit.

Two cases are treated apart. A failure at a known time needs the hazard at the moment it happened, and the midpoint of the interval it fell in is earlier and, in a ramp, cooler; so that interval is closed with a very short one ending at the failure. This is the larger of the two errors: without the closing interval, a ramp followed in intervals of a minute underestimated b = 1.7 by about 4% in a simulation of eight large assays, and with it b was recovered whatever the length of the intervals. A failure known only to the interval between two checks keeps that interval whole, since where in it the individual failed is not known, and its contribution is the probability of failing anywhere in it. Its hazard is still taken at its midpoint, and on a ramp checked at long intervals that is the largest error of all, because the grid cannot reduce it: in simulations of ramps of 0.1 to 0.3 degrees per minute checked every 3 minutes (failure intervals of 0.3 to 0.9 degrees), b was 3% low and sCTmax 0.07 degrees low at b = 1.7, and 20% and 0.23 degrees low at b = 4.7, whatever the step. A warning is given when temperature changes by more than half a degree within such an interval. On a ramp, check often enough that temperature changes by a few tenths of a degree at most between checks, the fewer the higher b, or record the time of each failure. A static assay is not affected, since temperature does not change within its intervals.

When neither checks nor grid_dt is given for failures at known times, the intervals are those between the readings of path, divided as above, and into at least 20 per individual, so that a trajectory given by its two ends is still followed closely.

Examples

# A single linear ramp encoded as two points: 20 -> 35 degrees over 60 minutes,
# with failure checked for every minute.
path   <- data.frame(path_id = "A", time = c(0, 60), temp = c(20, 35))
checks <- data.frame(path_id = "A", time = seq(0, 60, by = 1))

# Interval-censored: one failure found at the 30-minute check, one survivor.
ind <- data.frame(id = 1:2, path_id = "A", event = c(1, 0), t_upper = c(30, 60))
build_hazard_data(ind, path, "interval", checks = checks)

#>   short closing interval, so their hazard is that of the moment of failure.

# Known-time: the failure time itself, integrated on the same checks.
ind_c <- data.frame(id = 1, path_id = "A", event = 1, t_event = 42)
build_hazard_data(ind_c, path, "continuous", checks = checks)
